analysis.one_liner: Adds a 10-cent refundable deposit on beer and soda containers nationwide.
analysis.headline: Introduced with a single cosponsor, the bill was referred to the Senate Commerce Committee on January 28, 1997 and never received a hearing, vote, or any further action before the 105th Congress ended.
analysis.plain_summary: The bill would have put a 10-cent refundable deposit on beer, soda, wine cooler, and mineral water containers sold anywhere in the country, with the deposit rising with inflation every ten years. Consumers would get the 10 cents back for each container they returned, and unclaimed deposits would be paid to state governments to fund recycling and pollution-prevention programs rather than kept by beverage companies. It also banned pull-tab metal cans and the landfilling of container materials, and let states opt out if they had a similar law of their own or proved a 70 percent container recycling rate. It never reached a hearing or a vote.
analysis.who_benefits: Consumers who return containers get 10 cents back on each one. State governments would receive the unclaimed deposits to pay for pollution prevention and recycling programs. Communities gain from less litter and lower solid-waste disposal costs, and the recycling industry gains a steady, sorted supply of aluminum, glass, and plastic. The bill's findings state that state deposit laws have proven inexpensive to administer and effective at reducing financial burdens on communities.
analysis.who_benefits_short: Consumers, state recycling programs, and municipalities

how_it_helps.text: Every covered beverage container — beer, malt beverages, mineral water, soda water, wine coolers, and carbonated soft drinks in metal, glass, or plastic up to one gallon — would carry a 10-cent refund value that the retailer must pay back to anyone returning the empty container.

Unclaimed deposits would be paid by distributors to state governments each year and used for state pollution prevention and recycling programs, so money from containers never redeemed funds public programs rather than staying with the beverage industry.

The bill bans selling metal cans with detachable pull-tabs and bars retailers and distributors from dumping covered container material in landfills, and distributors must pay at least 2 cents per container in handling fees to people who return containers to them.

States are not forced into a one-size-fits-all scheme: a state with substantially similar requirements, or one that demonstrates a beverage container recycling or reuse rate of at least 70 percent for a year, is exempt.

The bill's own findings state that existing state deposit laws have proven inexpensive to administer and effective at reducing burdens on communities by internalizing recycling and litter costs to beverage producers and consumers rather than local governments and taxpayers.

analysis.who_pays: Beverage distributors and retailers bear the new costs of collecting deposits, storing and transporting returned containers, and paying refunds, with only a 2-cent handling fee to offset redemption costs. Beverage companies face labeling and reverse-logistics requirements. Consumers pay the 10 cents up front on every covered drink and recover it only by returning the container, so households that do not or cannot return containers effectively pay that amount into state recycling funds.
analysis.who_pays_short: Beverage distributors, retailers, and non-returning consumers

drawbacks.text: Retailers and grocers would have to collect a deposit on every covered sale, store the returned empties, and process redemptions; the bill provides no handling fee at all for retailer redemptions and only 2 cents per container when containers are returned to distributors instead.

Consumers pay the deposit up front and get it back only by returning containers, so people without convenient redemption access — including rural households or people without easy transportation — end up paying the 10 cents permanently, with the money routed to state programs.

Covered retailers and distributors face civil penalties of up to $1,000 per violation (up to $10,000 for failures to account for unclaimed refunds), and the scheme takes effect two years after enactment, requiring the entire beverage supply chain to rebuild collection and accounting systems on that timeline.

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The design is consumer-friendly for a deposit system: the deposit is fully refundable, unclaimed money goes to state recycling programs instead of industry, distributors owe a handling fee to people who return containers, and states can opt out with their own comparable law or a 70 percent recycling rate. The real costs fall on distributors and retailers, who take on collection, storage, and accounting work with only partial compensation, and on consumers who cannot easily return containers. Those costs are real but the bill's findings describe state-level versions of this system as inexpensive to administer; the larger honest caveat is that a national system would impose the burden on small grocers and convenience stores that state systems have also faced.

outcome.mechanism: The bill was referred to the Senate Commerce Committee the day it was introduced, the committee never held a hearing or vote on it, and it died when the 105th Congress ended in January 1999.

narrative.text: Senator Jim Jeffords of Vermont introduced the National Beverage Container Reuse and Recycling Act of 1997 on January 28, 1997.
The same day, the Senate read the bill twice and referred it to the Committee on Commerce, Science, and Transportation.
One Senate Democrat signed on as a cosponsor, but no further action was ever taken on the bill.
The Commerce Committee never scheduled a hearing or markup, no vote was ever held in either chamber, and the bill expired when the 105th Congress ended on January 3, 1999.

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Beverage bottlers, distributors, and retailers are better off, because they avoided a national 10-cent deposit and the collection, storage, and accounting costs that would have come with it. State recycling programs and communities that would have received unclaimed deposits and reduced litter costs gained nothing.

for.name: Sen. James Jeffords
for.what_they_did: Introduced the bill and delivered introductory remarks on the Senate floor.

against.name: Sen. John McCain
against.role: Chair, Senate Committee on Commerce, Science, and Transportation
against.what_they_did: Never scheduled the bill for a hearing, markup, or vote; it sat in committee from January 1997 until the Congress ended.

against.name: Beverage and grocery retail industry groups
against.role: Industry opponents of national container-deposit mandates
against.what_they_did: Have long opposed federal bottle-bill requirements, which force retailers to collect deposits and store and redeem returned containers.

sides.party_line_note: A Republican senator sponsored the bill with one Democratic cosponsor, and no committee or floor votes were ever cast, so the partisan shape of the issue was never tested.

industries.industry: Beverage bottlers and distributors (beer and soft drinks)
industries.note: They would have to print 10-cent refund values on containers, collect deposits down the distribution chain, handle returned empties, and pay each state the unclaimed refunds at year's end. The cost of building that reverse-collection system is the public's gain in recycling, litter reduction, and state program funding, so the industry's interest runs against the bill's purpose.

Retailers must collect the 10-cent deposit on every covered sale and pay it back on returns, with no handling fee for retailer redemptions, adding storage, labor, and accounting burden. That cost is what consumers gain back as refundable deposits.

A nationwide deposit plus a ban on landfilling container material would deliver a large, sorted, clean stream of aluminum, glass, and plastic to recyclers, and state unclaimed-deposit funds would bankroll recycling programs. What the industry gains, the public gains as reduced waste.
The bill bars retailers and distributors from disposing of covered containers or their metal, glass, or plastic in landfills, shrinking the material stream landfills and disposal facilities handle.
